title: arXiv AI papers — latest announcement batch, 11 November 2026
global_caveat: arXiv has no official trending chart; this is an inferred notable-paper ordering, and citation evidence is limited for papers announced today. No downloads, views, or citation gains during the window are claimed.

sections.title: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations
sections.abstract: The paper replaces testing a single hypothesis against its negation with mutually exclusive competing explanations, so evidence can identify an alternative as well as reject a claim.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors report that contrast sets resolved 67% more questions than pointwise surprisal under the same experiment budget; a blinded study of 38 experts agreed with the selected explanation on 78% of resolved questions.
sections.unique_caveat: Experiments use observational tabular data and one GPT-4o-based agent; resolution relies on LLM-elicited beliefs, and the authors note such findings are statistical rather than causal.

sections.title: One Policy for 100 Household Tasks: Our Solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge
sections.abstract: The authors describe a single vision-language-action checkpoint for 100 long-horizon household tasks in OmniGibson, report ninth place in the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge, and combine the learned policy with a coding agent on a subset of tasks.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors report one VLA checkpoint across 100 simulated household tasks, with Q=0.392 over all tasks; their public submission, which includes part of the coding-agent results on 14 tasks, scores Q=0.446 and 27.3% full-task success.
sections.unique_caveat: Results are from the OmniGibson simulator; the public submission included only part of the coding-agent results, so the reported agent and learned-policy figures are not a like-for-like full-task comparison.

sections.title: Earlybird: Predictive Streaming Speech Recognition in 29M Parameters
sections.abstract: Earlybird is a 29M-parameter streaming recognizer trained to predict words from partial speech, with the authors reporting a median correct word prediction 90 ms before it ends on LibriSpeech test-clean.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors report correct prediction of the median LibriSpeech test-clean word 90 ms before completion, earlier than the compared streaming models, and roughly ties a same-size competitor on English ASR accuracy.
sections.unique_caveat: Evaluation is English-only in the reported benchmarks; the abstract does not establish performance for other languages or noisy, real-world conversational conditions.

sections.title: ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows
sections.abstract: ReTrace converts an SOP and a few logged agent runs into a reusable code-driven workflow that replaces per-step LLM planning, reporting lower latency and cost with some task-success trade-offs.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors report 93.8% completion versus 96.8% for the agent on 79 procedures at 24% lower cost, and 75.8% success on tau-squared-Bench with 1.3-second execution versus 170 seconds for the agent.
sections.unique_caveat: Extracted reasoning may not reflect why an agent acted; tests concern new inputs to the same procedures rather than transfer to new procedures, and enterprise completion can be misreported by the platform.

sections.title: Agent Benchmarks Stop Ranking Before They Run Out of Tasks
sections.abstract: Re-scoring eight agent benchmarks, the paper argues that pass/fail scoring can hide meaningful differences between agents and proposes anchored graded scores with cost tracked separately.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors report that pass/fail ties can conceal more than tenfold differences in a Terminal-Bench re-run and propose a clipped log-ratio score with dated anchors and a separate cost axis.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors qualify several results: the sliding-window finding rests on ALE-Bench with partly reconstructed dates, and aggregate separation in their re-run is borderline across three trials.

sections.title: AutoScaffold: AI-Guided Scaffolding for Reinforcement Learning of Language Models
sections.abstract: AutoScaffold uses a frozen teacher to diagnose a student model’s RL training experience and adapt temporary strategies or hints, which are removed at evaluation.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors report improvements over the corresponding RL baselines in all four domains under scaffold-free evaluation, including +7.2 points in ALFWorld success and +4.0 points in average QA exact match.
sections.unique_caveat: The evidence comes from four task domains and specific student/teacher setups; wider transfer and the cost of repeated teacher interventions remain unestablished here.

sections.title: Re-Search: Dissecting LLM Ideation Through a Two-Player Questioning Game
sections.abstract: Re-Search tests research ideation as a Twenty Questions-style game over 200 ICML 2026 papers and finds that most of six tested LLMs make little progress after roughly 30 of 100 questions.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors’ controlled tests suggest candidate generation, rather than judging, is a bottleneck: weaker models improve when given externally proposed questions or a richer hypothesis space.
sections.unique_caveat: The testbed is 200 machine-learning papers from ICML 2026; recovery scores and search-tree annotations rely on LLM judges, and the authors say errors and possible self-preference cannot be fully ruled out.

sections.title: Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents
sections.abstract: The authors compare three evaluation frameworks on two analytics agents and report that trace-based judging balances precision and recall better than text-only judging, while functional testing and red-teaming expose different failures.
sections.claimed_contribution: In the authors’ controlled setting, trace-based evaluation reaches F1=0.90 on known risks, text-only evaluation produces five times more false alarms, and functional testing and security red-teaming find disjoint novel failures.
sections.unique_caveat: The study uses frozen traces from only two analytics agents, so it does not establish the same framework ordering for live agents or other task domains.
